documents.unit: Academic Senate, Council on Educational Policy
documents.title: Guidelines for Course Syllabi (Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy section)
documents.summary: The Academic Senate (CEP) syllabus guidelines require every syllabus to include a policy on student use of generative AI, state that there is no campus-wide policy, and leave content to the instructor. Tips ask instructors to set course- or assignment-level rules, explain how and why AI is or is not acceptable, point students to UCI tools such as ZotGPT, keep current with tool features, and explain the learning rationale, what counts as a violation, and how the policy is enforced.

units.anchor: All course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI
units.policy: All course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI in the course.

units.anchor: There is no general campus policy on student use of generative AI
the content of the policy is at the discretion of the instructor
units.policy: The content of each course's generative AI policy is at the discretion of the instructor.

units.anchor: Your policy should provide guidance at the course level and/or the assignment level.
whether using generative AI might facilitate or impede student learning in completing the tasks
units.policy: Instructors should consider the tasks in the course and each assignment (e.g., literature review, analysis, writing, grammar-check) and whether generative AI might facilitate or impede student learning in them.

units.anchor: it is important to have the most up-to-date understanding of those capabilities
units.policy: Because apps and platforms often update their features, instructors should have an up-to-date understanding of their capabilities before course delivery in case the policy needs updating.

units.anchor: Your syllabus should explain how and why using generative AI is or is not acceptable
units.policy: The syllabus should explain how and why using generative AI is or is not acceptable for the course, for each assignment, and/or for specific tasks within assignments.

units.anchor: There may be cases within the course where AI is a helpful learning tool
units.policy: Within a course there may be cases where AI is a helpful learning tool and others where it is strictly forbidden.

units.anchor: Differentiating among these cases will guide student efforts.
encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as ZotGPT
units.policy: If the policy allows AI, instructors should encourage students to use UCI-specific AI resources, such as ZotGPT and other UCI-built tools, when possible.

units.anchor: explain what aspects of learning the policy is intended to safeguard
units.policy: To bolster understanding and adherence, instructors should explain what aspects of learning the AI policy is intended to safeguard.

units.anchor: explain what constitutes a violation of academic integrity
units.policy: Instructors should explain what constitutes a violation of academic integrity under their AI policy.

units.anchor: Describe how the policy will be enforced in the course.
For non-exhaustive examples of syllabi language and other resources
units.policy: Instructors are referred to non-exhaustive examples of AI syllabus language and resources from UCI DTEI and other universities.

documents.unit: Division of Teaching Excellence and Innovation (Office of the Vice Provost for Teaching and Learning)
documents.title: Generative AI: Is my AI policy - and the rationale - clear on the syllabus?
documents.summary: DTEI restates the Senate requirement for undergraduate syllabi and the Graduate Council policy (effective February 12, 2026) that every graduate syllabus include a generative-AI policy set by the instructor. It explains that the lack of a campus-wide policy is deliberate because AI's role differs by discipline, and expects instructors to write a clear course-specific policy, communicate it in the syllabus, and apply it transparently and consistently.

units.anchor: all undergraduate course syllabi include a clear statement addressing the use of generative AI
units.policy: Academic Senate guidance requires that all undergraduate course syllabi include a clear statement addressing the use of generative AI tools.

units.anchor: All graduate course syllabi must include a policy on student use of generative AI

the content of each policy is left to the discretion of the instructor

units.policy: Graduate programs are expected to include the syllabus AI-policy requirement, with appropriate language, in their program handbooks.

units.anchor: the absence of a single campuswide policy is intentional
units.policy: The absence of a single campuswide AI policy is intentional.

units.anchor: The pedagogical role of generative AI varies significantly across disciplines, course levels, and learning objectives.

limited or prohibited to preserve specific learning outcomes or forms of assessment
units.policy: In other contexts, AI use may be limited or prohibited to preserve specific learning outcomes or forms of assessment.

units.policy: Because of this variation, instructors are best positioned to define appropriate AI use within their own courses.

units.anchor: Develop a clear, course-specific policy on student use of generative AI

units.policy: All instructors are expected to ensure that AI expectations are transparent and consistently applied.

units.policy: DTEI recognizes that generative AI in teaching is an evolving space.

units.anchor: align your course policies with your learning goals and values as educators
units.policy: Instructors are encouraged to use this as an opportunity to align their course AI policies with their learning goals and values as educators.

documents.title: Syllabus Policies Governing Student Use of AI (five example statements)
tiers: Example 2 — AI Used Only for Editing and Grammar Check
Example 3 — AI Use OK with Caveats
Example 4 — AI: Use…But Cite and Explain
Example 5 — AI Encouraged…with Guardrails and Caveats
documents.summary: A DTEI-curated document of five adaptable syllabus statements on a spectrum: AI prohibited, editing and grammar check only, allowed with acknowledgment, ZotGPT for listed tasks with citation and reflection, and AI expected with guardrails. The templates cover learning rationale, inaccuracy and bias, disclosure details (tool, prompt, revisions, reflection), meetings and knowledge checks when misuse is suspected, and prompting as a skill. Template units are coded with the student as actor because the statements are addressed to students.

they can and should be adapted for specific assignments based on your pedagogical rationale

documents.unit: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences
documents.title: ICS 33 Fall 2026, Course Reference
documents.summary: ICS 33 (Thornton) prohibits generative AI so that students build their own programming skills first, and says asking AI to write any part of a solution is academic dishonesty. All submissions go through automated plagiarism detection and violations are reported to AISC, with a possible course F. A 'humanity pledge' commits the instructor to write all his own communication and asks students to do the same.

units.anchor: When I'm communicating with you, it will be me (and me alone) doing that communicating
units.policy: When the instructor communicates with students (lecture, Zoom, email, web site, Canvas), it will be the instructor alone doing that communicating, not generative AI.

units.anchor: educational experience we're engaging in is the humanity at its center
units.policy: The fundamental value of the educational experience is the humanity at its center.

units.anchor: we can only do that if you're willing to exercise them
units.policy: Staff are there to help students develop communication skills, which is only possible if students exercise those skills themselves.

units.anchor: those words should be yours (and yours alone)
units.policy: Words students send to course staff for a human response should be the student's own, not AI-generated.

units.anchor: let's have it be a two-way human conversation
units.policy: Course communication between students and staff should be a two-way human conversation.

units.anchor: the use of generative AI tools is prohibited in this course
The primary educational goal is developing one's own programming skills
units.policy: The primary educational goal is developing one's own programming skills, which can't be done if someone else is doing the heavy lifting.

units.anchor: you'll surely have opportunities to learn about the use of generative AI tools
units.policy: Students will have opportunities later to learn about the use of generative AI tools.

units.anchor: I use as a force multiplier on my own skills quite literally every day
units.policy: The instructor discloses using generative AI tools daily in other work as a force multiplier on his own skills.

units.anchor: it's necessary for you to build your skills first
units.policy: Students must build their skills first, by which time they will find AI tools vastly more useful.

units.anchor: All of your work on projects and reinforcement exercises is expected to be completed
units.policy: All work on projects and reinforcement exercises is expected to be completed solely by the student.

units.anchor: this disallows the use of automatic systems, such as generative AI systems like ChatGPT
units.policy: Using automatic systems such as generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) to produce any part of a solution is disallowed, because that would not be code written solely by the student.

units.anchor: All submissions are compared to one another using an automated plagiarism detection system.
All violations of academic honesty policies will be reported to the
units.policy: All violations of academic honesty policies will be reported to the UCI Office of Academic Integrity & Student Conduct (AISC).

units.anchor: you can receive a course grade of F
units.policy: Students who violate academic honesty can receive a course grade of F without the option to drop the course.

units.anchor: A single documented case of academic dishonesty may also have other ramificiations
units.policy: A single documented case of academic dishonesty may preclude switching into computing majors, computing minors, the ICS Honors Program, and graduating with honors.

units.anchor: Did you actually write the code in question?
units.policy: The test for dishonesty is whether the student actually wrote the code, i.e., whether it comprises their own ideas about solving the problem and organizing the solution.

units.anchor: ask a generative AI system to write a solution to some or all
units.policy: Asking a generative AI system to write a solution to some or all of an assignment crosses the line into academic dishonesty.

units.anchor: We require you to do your own work, because that's how the learning is done
if someone else is making most of those decisions for you, that's plagiarism

new_types.name: Human-written course communication
new_types.definition: Messages exchanged between students and course staff (emails, posts, questions sent for a human reply) are to be written by the person sending them, not generated by AI, so that course communication stays a human-to-human exchange. Distinct from P18 (which splits permissions for AI-written prose versus code) and from P19 (which governs submitted work); the instructor-side pledge is coded P47.

notes: Reconciled consensus of two independent coders (v2 dry run). Collection notes: University layer: there is intentionally no campuswide policy on student AI use; the Senate CEP syllabus guidelines require an AI policy in every syllabus at instructor discretion, and DTEI pages restate this. The DTEI example-statements Google Doc was fetched through fetch_text's Google Docs export route. Excluded: OVPTL 'ChatGPT FAQs 6 Months In' (2023 message aimed at writing instructors; https://ovptl.uci.edu/news/chatgpt-faqs-6-months-in-a-campuswide-message-from-ovptl-and-the-campus-writing-communication-coordinator/, file v2-uc-irvine-ovptl-faq); OAISC faculty page (https://conduct.uci.edu/academic-integrity-info-for-faculty-staff/, file v2-uc-irvine-oaisc), whose only AI text is optional sample language for writing classes; DTEI hub and assessment pages (links only). School/computing: the Bren School of ICS is the combined school-and-computing unit (departments of Computer Science, Informatics, Statistics); no ICS-, department-, or Samueli School/EECS-level AI policy found. Course layer: both courses are by the same instructor (Thornton), whose pages are the only public Fall 2026 ICS syllabi found. CS 175 syllabus (uc-irvine-cs175.github.io) checked: no AI policy. Informatics, Statistics/data science, and EECS course syllabi appear to sit in Canvas; none public found. Reconciliation details and the rationale for each resolved disagreement are in v2/dryrun/agreement_uc-irvine.json.
